title: Understanding and Mitigating Numerical Sources of Nondeterminism in LLM In

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text cites "benchmarking and evaluation ... reliability, safety, and fairness [7, 40]", but the reference list ends at [39]. Reference [40] does not exist.

predicted_errors.error_location: Preliminaries, paragraph on deterministic libraries and random seeds
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The claim about PyTorch/TensorFlow deterministic flags is cited as "torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True) [2]". But reference [2] is the GPT-4 Technical Report, not PyTorch documentation or a source for that API.

The paper explicitly states: "Experiments occasionally employ non-identical random seeds during greedy decoding." This invalidates the claimed attribution of greedy-output differences to numerical precision and runtime configuration alone. Differences in seeds are an uncontrolled confound, despite the surrounding claims of fixed-seed greedy experiments.

LayerCast is first defined as storing BF16 weights and "performing computations without upcasting to FP32 at runtime." The immediately following paragraph says the method "ensures all computations occur in full FP32 precision." These are mutually incompatible descriptions of the core method.

The text says Table 26 shows LayerCast has "occasional stochastic fluctuations around 0.2–0.5% Std@Acc." However, every LayerCast value in Table 26 is exactly 36.67% across all 12 configurations. Thus its displayed standard deviation is zero, not 0.2–0.5%.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 5 versus Table 23, MATH500 / Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct / BF16
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 5 reports a MATH500 BF16 standard deviation of 0.4663% for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Table 23 instead lists BF16 MATH500 accuracies of 90.65, 91.15, 90.40, 90.95, 90.85, and 90.35, whose displayed standard deviation is 0.3158%, not 0.4663%. Those six BF16 values and 0.3158% standard deviation are an exact duplicate of the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B MATH500 row shown in the preceding random-sampling table, indicating a copied/mislabeled result.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix G, opening paragraph versus Table 5 and Tables 21–24
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Appendix G says: "The standard deviations are calculated across numeric precision types (BF16, FP16, FP32)." In contrast, Table 5 explicitly says its standard deviations are across six system configurations, and Tables 21–24 calculate one standard deviation separately within each precision row across six GPU-count/batch-size configurations. The appendix statement describes a different calculation.

The appendix says Div_Index is "in the 0–1 range" and that 1 means tokenwise-identical responses. But Table 8 reports Div_Index values such as 45.67, 430.13, 1825.79, and 5807.83. This directly contradicts the stated range and also conflicts with the main-text definition of Div_Index as a token position.

The paper claims Table 15 shows that "larger batch sizes consistently lead to lower Avg_Std@top1_prob." The table does not support consistency. Examples include AIME'24 BF16 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (30.81, 36.82, 34.41 for batch sizes 8, 16, 32), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (35.88, 32.09, 37.75), and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (53.86, 58.55, 47.23). In each case the sequence is non-monotonic, and larger batch size sometimes increases the reported instability.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.2 and Conclusion, claims that FP32 provides near-perfect/negligible-variance determinism
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text says FP32 "consistently achieves near-perfect reproducibility with negligible variance" and the conclusion says FP32 provides "near-perfect determinism." Yet the paper's own tables show non-negligible FP32 variability: Table 6 reports FP32 Std@Acc up to 0.78% on LiveCodeBench-Medium and 0.53% on LiveCodeBench-Hard; Table 7 reports FP32 output-length variability up to 690.86 tokens; Table 9 reports FP32 divergent-output rates up to 30.08%; Table 10 reports 1.11% FP32 Std@Acc for Qwen3-32B; and Table 11 reports 1.96% for GPQA Diamond. FP32 improves reproducibility, but the universal near-determinism characterization is not supported.

The paper says that because Table 5 standard deviations are across configurations, they "largely reflect the impact from limited numerical precision, not the inherent variance of models." But each configuration's reported Pass@1 is itself estimated from only 4, 16, or 64 random samples. Without matched sampling seeds, repeated runs within each configuration, or a variance decomposition, cross-configuration variation necessarily mixes numerical/configuration effects with Monte-Carlo sampling variation. The stated attribution is unsupported by the design.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix H, theoretical justification of LayerCast
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The appendix states that just-in-time BF16-to-FP32 casting is deterministic and "introduces no additional variance," then immediately says LayerCast may show "minor numerical instability due to dynamic casting operations." These explanations are contradictory: if deterministic casts introduce no variance, dynamic casting cannot be the proposed source of stochastic fluctuations.
